title: Work with Electrical Components and Systems

lessons.title: Batteries, wiring and the multimeter
lessons.html:
Working safely with tractor electrics

A tractor battery is 12 V, which will not normally shock you, but it can deliver very high current. A spanner across the terminals can glow red hot, burn you and make the battery explode.

Battery safety

  • Wear safety glasses and gloves. Battery acid burns skin and eyes.
  • No sparks, flames or smoking near batteries. They give off hydrogen gas.
  • To disconnect: remove the negative lead first. To connect: fit the negative lead last.
  • Lift batteries with a carrier and keep them upright.
  • If acid gets in your eyes, rinse with lots of clean water and get medical help.

Checking a battery

  1. Look for cracks, leaks and corroded terminals.
  2. Clean terminals with a wire brush and protect them with terminal grease.
  3. Check the battery is clamped tight.
  4. Measure voltage with a multimeter with the engine off. Compare with the battery maker's chart to see the state of charge.

Using a multimeter

A multimeter measures volts, amps and ohms.

  • Volts: set to DC volts, red lead on positive, black on negative or earth.
  • Ohms (resistance): only on a circuit with no power. Use it to check fuses, bulbs and wires for continuity.
  • Amps: the meter must be in series with the circuit. Ask your mechanic before measuring current; the wrong setting can blow the meter fuse.

Wires, fuses and connectors

Wires are colour-coded and sized for their current. Fuses protect wires. Always fit a fuse of the same rating. Check connectors for corrosion, loose pins and broken locks.

lessons.title: Lights, starters and alternators
lessons.html:
Common electrical jobs

Lights

Tractors need working head lights, work lights, tail lights, brake lights, indicators and hazard lights, especially when driving on public roads. To fix a light that does not work:

  1. Check the bulb or LED unit. Replace with the same type and wattage.
  2. Check the fuse.
  3. Check for voltage at the lamp connector with the switch on.
  4. Check the earth wire is clean and tight.
  5. Look for broken or chafed wires.

Starting system

The starting system has the battery, key switch, neutral safety switch, starter relay or solenoid and starter motor. If the tractor does not crank:

  • Check battery voltage and terminals first.
  • Check the gear lever is in neutral or park.
  • Listen for a click from the solenoid.
  • Ask the mechanic before testing further. Never bypass the neutral safety switch or start the tractor by shorting the starter terminals; the tractor can drive over you.

Charging system

The alternator charges the battery when the engine runs. It is driven by a belt. Signs of trouble: the charge warning light stays on, lights are dim, the battery goes flat. Check the belt tension and condition first, then measure battery voltage with the engine running and compare with the manual.

Replacing a part

  1. Disconnect the battery negative lead.
  2. Label wires before removing them.
  3. Fit the new part and tighten terminals firmly, not too tight.
  4. Reconnect the battery and test the system.

Protecting wiring

Route wires away from hot exhausts and sharp edges. Use cable ties and clips. Seal connectors against water and dust. On farms, rats and mice chew wires in parked tractors, so check wiring on tractors that stood for a long time.

Key points

  • Remove the battery negative first and refit it last.
  • Keep sparks and flames away from batteries.
  • Measure resistance only with the power off.
  • Fit fuses and bulbs of the same rating.
  • Never bypass the neutral safety switch.
